That record holds John Wentworth's 1881 address as a document - Fergus' Historical Series No. 16 - and is the one to cite for anything about the fort. This record holds the chicagology PAGE that reprints it: the same text, reached by URL, graded as the modern compilation it is. Both were written on 2026-08-11 by agents working different parcels who did not know of each other, and they agree on the substance, including both of the guards below; the difference in tier (2 against 4) and rights (public_domain against check_required) is the difference between grading the 1881 pamphlet and grading the 2020s web page carrying it, not a disagreement about the evidence. THE DOSSIERS CITE THIS PAGE BY THIS NAME - docs/research/04-structures-south.md tags five claims '[DOC] chicagology prefire052' and docs/research/08-fauna.md a sixth - which is the only reason this id exists. If you arrived here from a dossier, take the fort dimensions from wentworth_1881_fort_dearborn and never from both. What follows is the page as read at its URL, and the parts of it that lie outside the fort proper (Beaubien's 1835 purchase, the lighthouse note) are the only content here that record does not already carry.

THE ONLY DIMENSIONAL EVIDENCE THIS PROJECT HAS REACHED FOR THE INSIDE OF FORT DEARBORN, and it is a caption to a photograph taken TWENTY YEARS after the scene date. Verbatim: "Wood cut from a photo taken in 1855 by Alex. Hesler, from the U. S. Marine Hospital, looking north-west, correctly represents two of the principal buildings of the Fort - the Commandant's Quarters, (A) (brick, about 25x50 ft.), and the Officers' Quarters, (B) (wood, about 30x60 ft,), occupying the north-west corner of the enclosure. (C) is the parade-ground (80x200 ft.); (D) is the Sutler's; (E) is the north gate." The circled letters are rendered here as parentheses; the stray comma inside "30x60 ft," is the page's.

THE PAGE CONTRADICTS ITSELF ON THE PARADE GROUND, AND THE DOSSIER CARRIED ONLY ONE HALF OF IT. The 1855 caption says 80x200 ft. The Fergus addendum on the same page, describing the fort in 1850, says: "The parade-ground was between the commandant's, officers', and sutler's quarters on the west, and the building where the artillery was housed, the soldier's barracks, and the storehouse on the east; and was about 80 feet wide, and extended from the river bank south, the full length of the enclosure - say 400 feet." Eighty by two hundred and eighty by four hundred are not the same rectangle. Both figures are approximations ("about", "say") recalled from views of a fort already two decades past the scene date. docs/research/04-structures-south.md records "Parade ground ~80 x 200 ft" as [DOC] from this page; the 200 is attested, the exclusivity is not. Model the parade ground as INFERRED with the disagreement recorded, not as documented.

WHAT THE FERGUS ADDENDUM DOES SETTLE, for 1850 and no earlier: the arrangement of the parade ground between quarters on the west and artillery house, barracks and storehouse on the east; "another building in the Fort enclosure ... just east of the block-house ... was the quartermaster's or sutler's quarters" (his own "or" - he is not sure which); the sun-dial, "an 8-inch piece of square timber, imbedded in the earth, placed upright, about 2 feet high, upon the top of which was a brass plate on which had been a sun-dial", on a knoll near the parade ground's southern end; a turn-stile about 100 feet south of it entering from the centre of Michigan Avenue; "The whole Fort enclosure was surrounded by a rough-board fence, white-washed, about 6 feet high; the pickets having been removed at an earlier date"; and "The kitchen-garden was in the south-west corner of the enclosure."

A GUARD THE DOSSIERS NEED. The page's two extended PHYSICAL descriptions of the fort are of the WRONG FORT and the WRONG DECADE. The Chicago Magazine (March 1857) passage - two blockhouses at the south-east and north-west corners, the sally-port or subterranean passage on the north side leading from the parade ground to the river, the strong palisade of wooden pickets, the two-story log United States factory west of the fort, the root-houses between fort and factory, the garden on the south side, three pieces of light artillery, and "A company of United-States troops, about fifty in number, many of whom were invalids" - closes with the sentence "Such was the old Fort previous to 1812." It is the FIRST fort. The Fergus addendum is the fort in 1850. Neither is 1835. docs/research/04-structures-south.md line 49 tags the sally-port [DOC] from this page "attested for the 1816 fort's north side", and docs/research/08-fauna.md line 200 takes the fifty invalids and the enclosed and cultivated garden from this page as 1835-relevant; on this page both passages are pre-1812. The only sally-port sentence that could be about the 1816 fort is John H. Kinzie's, quoted higher up - "Although it stood upon the same ground as the last Fort, it was differently constructed, having two block-houses on the southern side; and on the northern side, a sally-port, or subterranean passage from the parade ground to the river" - and Wentworth places it inside his discussion of the ORIGINAL fort's plan, so which fort "it" names is not decidable from this page. Two of the three descriptions also disagree about where the blockhouses were (southern side versus south-east and north-west corners).

NO HOSPITAL BUILDING. docs/research/04-structures-south.md line 48 lists a "hospital" among the fort's structures, [DOC] from this page. There is no hospital building on this page. What there is, is the War Department return quoted for the 1832 cholera - "Fort Dearborn having become a general hospital on July 11th, no returns were received until its reoccupation" - which is a USE of the fort, not a building in it. (The U. S. Marine Hospital named in the 1855 caption is the vantage point of the photograph, built after 1848 on the reservation, and is not a fort building either.)

OTHER THINGS THIS PAGE SETTLES. The last commandant, Bvt. Maj. Joseph Plympton, arrived 1 August 1836 and stayed to June or July 1837, "although the soldiers were withdrawn on December 29th, 1836", per Macomb's order of 30 November 1836. On 28 May 1835 J. B. Beaubien bought the entire Fort Dearborn Reservation for $94.61 - inside the scene year, five weeks before the scene date. Wentworth locates Beaubien's later house explicitly: "If you wish to find the traditional residence of Gen. Jean Baptiste Beaubien, after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house, go east upon South-Water Street until you come to the north-east corner of South-Water Street and Michigan Ave." That "after he moved" is the hinge of the dossier's unresolved SW-versus-NE corner - see chicagology_prefire276. The Chicago Magazine (March 1857) lighthouse note also appears here: "A lighthouse was established here, by an Act of Congress, March 3, 1831. It fell soon after completion, in October of that year; but it was soon rebuilt. Samuel C. Lasby was the first keeper."
